analysis.one_liner: Requires the IRS to audit every president's tax returns and post the returns and audit reports online.
analysis.headline: The House passed it 222–201 two days after introduction, with 217 of 218 Democrats in favor, but the Senate never voted and it died when the Congress ended on January 3, 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require the IRS to examine a president's income tax return as quickly as practicable after it is filed, then publish the return itself online along with an initial report within 90 days, periodic updates during the audit, and a final report describing every proposed adjustment and how it was resolved [S2][S4]. It would cover the returns of the president and the president's spouse, plus any corporation, partnership, trust, or estate they control or benefit from, and it would apply to amended returns and to failures to file [S4]. It carves this transparency requirement out of the normal rule that tax returns are confidential, with redactions for Social Security numbers, account numbers, minors' names, and IRS employee names [S4]. The House passed it in the final days of the 117th Congress; the Senate received it but never voted, so it expired.
analysis.who_benefits: Voters and taxpayers, who would be able to read a sitting president's actual tax returns and audit results online within weeks of filing, rather than relying on voluntary disclosures. The public would learn within 90 days whether an examination had even begun, and would see each proposed adjustment, any dispute over it, and how it ended [S4]. Future presidents who own or control businesses would face the same published scrutiny, closing a rule that until now was an informal practice a president could ignore.

how_it_helps.text: Requires the IRS to examine each presidential income tax return 'as rapidly as practicable' after filing, replacing a voluntary audit practice with a legal requirement.

Requires the IRS to publish the return itself, an initial report within 90 days, periodic reports at least every 180 days, and a final report listing each proposed adjustment and controversy and how it was resolved.

Covers not just the president and spouse but also corporations, partnerships, trusts, and estates they control or benefit from, including amendments and failures to file, and excludes Social Security and account numbers and minors' names from what is published.
Requires a public report whenever a president requests a filing extension, and treats a failure to file as triggering the same audit and public reports.
Passed the House with a near party-line vote of 222–201 on December 22, 2022.

analysis.who_pays: Sitting presidents and presidential candidates with business holdings, whose tax returns, business entities, and complete audit files would become public record, including disputes with the IRS even when no wrongdoing is found. Presidents' spouses, business partners, and trust beneficiaries would have their tax information published as well. The IRS would take on ongoing examination and public-reporting work for every presidential return.

drawbacks.text: The bill publishes audit materials for entities controlled by a president or spouse, including trusts and estates where they are beneficiaries, so business associates and family members' financial information enters the public record even though identifying numbers and minors' names are redacted.
A president who faces a proposed IRS adjustment that is later withdrawn or resolved without any change would still have the dispute and its details permanently published online.

The bill was introduced December 21, 2022 and passed the House the next day under a rule that closed it to amendments, leaving no opportunity to refine who is covered or what is redacted before the Congress ended.
Because it took effect only after enactment, it would not have applied to any return already filed by a sitting president.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is a clear one for accountability: the one office with the most concentrated power would lose the ability to keep its tax filings and audit outcomes secret, and the requirement would apply automatically to every future president rather than depending on voluntary release. The costs are real but narrower: some financial information about presidents' families, partners, and trust beneficiaries becomes public, and audit disputes that resolve in the president's favor are published anyway. The main design weakness is the process, not the content — a bill with this reach was drafted and passed in two days with no amendments allowed, so Congress never worked through the edge cases.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it 222–201 on December 22, 2022, two days after it was introduced, but the Senate only received the bill and never brought it to a vote before the Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on December 21, 2022 and referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the same day.
The Rules Committee reported a resolution providing one hour of debate, a closed rule barring amendments, and a motion to recommit; the House considered it under that rule on December 22.
The House passed the bill by a recorded vote of 222–201, with 217 of 218 Democrats voting yes and 201 of 213 Republicans voting no; only 5 Republicans supported it.
The Senate received the bill on December 22, 2022, and no further action was taken before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Sitting and future presidents keep the ability to withhold their tax returns and audit files from the public; the confidentiality of presidential tax information stayed intact. The IRS's existing discretionary practice — which allowed one president to break with decades of voluntary disclosure without legal consequence — remains unchanged.

for.name: Richard E. Neal
for.role: Sponsor, House Ways and Means Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on December 21, 2022, the final week of the Congress.

against.name: Senate
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on December 22, 2022 and took no further action before the Congress ended; no senator brought it to a vote.

sides.party_line_note: The vote split almost entirely by party: 217 of 218 Democrats voted yes and 201 of 213 Republicans voted no, with just 5 Republicans in support.

industries.note: The bill's direct cost falls on presidents and their controlled corporations, partnerships, trusts, and estates, whose tax returns and full audit files would be posted online. Its interest in keeping that information confidential runs against the public's interest in verifying the tax compliance of the officeholder.

industries.industry: Tax law and accounting firms serving presidents and political figures
industries.note: Audit materials, proposed adjustments, and IRS correspondence for presidential filings would become public, exposing the positions firms take on behalf of presidents. Most of the profession is unaffected; the burden is confined to work for the president and the president's family.
